passages.happening:
“We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves” (verse 1). “Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to build him up” (verse 2).

“For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written: ‘The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me’” (verse 3).

What was written in the past was written to teach us, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (verse 4). Paul prays that the God who gives endurance and encouragement will give them harmony with one another in Christ Jesus (verse 5), “so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Paul finishes the argument he began in chapter 14. He puts himself among ‘the strong’, those who believed they were free to eat anything. Then he tells the strong that their strength is for carrying others, not for getting their own way.

‘Bear with’ means carry, as you would carry a load for someone. ‘Not to please ourselves’ cuts against the way most people lived. In Rome, as everywhere, the strong expected the weak to make room for them. Paul turns it around.

His reason is Christ. Christ had every right to please himself, and he did not. He took insults that were not his to take. If he carried that for us, the strong can carry a brother's scruples about food.

Notice where the passage ends: one mind and one voice, praising God together. The goal is not that one side wins the argument. It is a church whose Jewish and Gentile members can worship side by side.
passages.ot:
Verse 3 quotes Psalm 69, the prayer of a righteous man who suffers for his loyalty to God: “because zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me” (Psalm 69:9). The psalmist bore shame because he belonged to God. The site's note on Psalm 69 shows how the New Testament reads this psalm of Jesus: John quotes the first half of this verse, and Paul quotes the second half here.

Verse 4 says why Paul can use the psalm this way. The Scriptures of Israel were written ‘for our instruction’. They are not only Israel's history. They give hope to every believer who reads them with endurance.
passages.asks: Paul says the strong should carry the weak. Ask where you are strong: in knowledge, money, health, confidence or position. Then ask whose load you could carry this week, in a way that builds that person up and does not only please you.

passages.t: ‘Accept one another’: the Gentiles praise God
passages.happening:
“Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God” (verse 7).

Christ became a servant of the circumcised, the Jewish people, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs (verse 8), “so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy” (verse 9).

Then Paul gives four Scriptures in a row. “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name” (verse 9). “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people” (verse 10). “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples” (verse 11). And Isaiah says, “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope” (verse 12).

“Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘Accept one another’ is where Paul has been heading since chapter 14. If Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome had grown apart, and some had begun to meet separately, this is Paul's plea to come back to one table. The book page sets out the likely history behind it, as a reconstruction.

The reason he gives is Christ's own welcome. Christ did not wait for either group to become worthy. He came as a servant to the Jewish people, keeping God's promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And through him the Gentiles, the nations, came to praise God for mercy they had never been promised in the same way.

So the two groups owe their place to the same Christ. The Jewish believer cannot say Gentiles are second class; God promised long ago that they would praise him. The Gentile believer cannot look down on Jewish practice; Christ himself came as a servant to the circumcised.

Verse 13 is a prayer that gathers the letter's great words: hope, joy, peace, faith, and the power of the Spirit.
passages.ot:
Paul's four quotations come from every part of Israel's Scriptures: the Psalms, the Law and the Prophets. Each names the Gentiles, the nations.

The first is from David's song of victory, found twice: “Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name” (Psalm 18:49), and the same in 2 Samuel 22:50. David, king of Israel, praises God in front of the nations.

The second is from the Song of Moses at the end of the Law: “Rejoice, O nations, with His people” (Deuteronomy 32:43). Gentiles rejoice with Israel, not in place of Israel.

The third is the shortest psalm: “Praise the LORD, all you nations! Extol Him, all you peoples!” (Psalm 117:1).

The fourth is Isaiah's promise of a king from David's family, a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David's father: “On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples” (Isaiah 11:10). Paul follows the Greek translation, which speaks of one who will rise to rule the nations, in whom they will hope.
passages.hard:
Does ‘a servant of the circumcised’ mean that Christ came only for the Jews, or that Jewish believers today should give up their customs? Paul says neither. Christ came first as a servant to Israel, to keep God's promises to them (verse 8), and his coming also brought the Gentiles to praise God (verse 9). Paul does not ask Jewish believers to stop being Jews, or Gentile believers to become Jews. He asks them to accept one another.

Christians have read the relation of Israel and the church in different ways; the note on 11:11-16 sets out the main views. On any reading, this passage pictures Jews and Gentiles praising God together, and it gives no room for contempt in either direction.
passages.asks: ‘Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you.’ Think of a believer you find it hard to accept, because of background, habits or opinions. Ask how Christ accepted you. Then take one step toward that person this week.

passages.t: Paul's priestly service, from Jerusalem to Illyricum
passages.happening:
Paul says he is sure the Romans are full of goodness and knowledge and able to teach one another (verse 14). Still, he has written boldly on some points (verse 15), because of the grace God gave him “to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit” (verse 16).

He will speak only of what Christ has done through him to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed, by signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit (verses 18-19). “So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ” (verse 19).

His aim has been to preach where Christ was not known, “so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation” (verse 20). As Scripture says, “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Paul is polite here. He did not found the Roman churches, and he knows it. So he praises them before he explains why he has written so boldly.

Then he pictures his work as a priest's work. In the temple in Jerusalem, priests offered sacrifices to God. Gentiles could not go beyond the outer court. Paul says the Gentiles themselves are now his offering to God, made holy not by temple washing but by the Holy Spirit. The people once kept out are now the gift brought in.

‘From Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum’ sums up more than twenty years of travel. Illyricum was the Roman province along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, north and west of Macedonia. Acts does not tell of a visit there. Paul may mean he reached its border while travelling through Macedonia. The site's map of Romans shows Corinth, Rome and Jerusalem; Illyricum lies mostly beyond its top edge.

‘Fully proclaimed’ does not mean that every person in those lands had heard. It means Paul had planted churches in the key cities, from which the message could spread.
passages.ot:
Verse 21 quotes Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: “For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard” (Isaiah 52:15). In Isaiah, nations and kings are astonished at the servant who suffers and is lifted up. Paul sees that happening as Gentiles hear of Christ for the first time.

The picture of Gentiles as an offering also echoes Isaiah, who sees the nations bringing Israel's scattered people home “as a gift to the LORD” (Isaiah 66:20), “just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD” (Isaiah 66:20).
passages.asks: Paul's whole life was an offering: people brought to God. Ask what your work, whatever it is, could offer to God. Is there someone near you who has never been told about Christ, to whom you might be the first to speak?

passages.happening:
This work is why Paul has been hindered from coming to Rome (verse 22). But now there is no more room for him in these regions, and he has longed for years to visit (verse 23). “I hope to see you on my way to Spain” (verse 24), and to be sent on by them.

First he must go to Jerusalem to serve the saints (verse 25). “For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (verse 26). They owed it, he says: if the Gentiles have shared Israel's spiritual blessings, they should share their material blessings with them (verse 27). After he delivers the gift, he will go to Spain by way of Rome (verse 28).

He asks them to join his struggle in prayer (verse 30): “Pray that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there” (verse 31). Then he hopes to come to them with joy (verse 32). “The God of peace be with all of you. Amen” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The ‘contribution’ was a collection of money Paul had gathered for years from his Gentile churches in Greece and elsewhere for poor believers in Jerusalem. He writes about it in other letters too. In 1 Corinthians he tells them to set aside money on the first day of every week (1 Corinthians 16:1-3). Two whole chapters of 2 Corinthians, 8 and 9, are about it.

For Paul it was more than charity. It showed that Gentile and Jewish believers were one family. The Gentiles had received the riches of Israel's promises; now they gave back. In that world, gifts created bonds between giver and receiver.

Paul knew there was danger. He feared the unbelievers in Judea. And he was not sure the Jewish believers in Jerusalem would accept a gift from Gentiles gathered by him. Acts later says that many of them had heard he taught Jews to give up the law of Moses (Acts 21:21). So he asks for prayer.

What happened next? Acts tells that Paul did bring the gift. Later, before the Roman governor, he said, “I returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to my people” (Acts 24:17). But at the temple a crowd was stirred up against him and he was seized, and the Roman commander arrested him (Acts 21:27-33). He was held for two years at Caesarea, and he reached Rome, as he had hoped, but as a prisoner (Acts 28).

Did he ever reach Spain? The New Testament does not say. The letter called 1 Clement, written from Rome and usually dated near the end of the first century, speaks of Paul reaching, it says, the limits of the west. What that phrase means is argued: Rome, or Spain. It is tradition, and it is uncertain.
passages.ot:
Paul's idea that the Gentiles owe Israel a debt goes back to God's promise to Abraham: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The blessing came to the nations through Abraham's family, and through the Messiah born of it.

The prophets also pictured the wealth of the nations flowing to Jerusalem in the last days. Isaiah sees the nations bringing gifts, and bringing Israel's scattered people home “as a gift to the LORD” (Isaiah 66:20). Some readers think Paul saw his collection as a small sign of that hope. Paul himself does not say so here.
passages.hard:
Paul asked the believers in Rome to pray that he would be delivered from danger in Judea. Yet he was arrested, held for years, and came to Rome in chains. Was the prayer not answered?

Christians have answered in different ways. Some note that Paul was in fact delivered from death more than once in Acts 21 to 28, and that he did come to Rome, and did come ‘with joy’ in his own way, preaching openly there (Acts 28:30-31). Others say simply that God sometimes answers ‘not like this’, and that the plan Paul made was not the plan God carried out. Both agree that Paul's plans were held under ‘by God's will’ (verse 32). Paul did not pretend to know the future. He asked for prayer and went.
passages.asks: Paul made plans and held them open to God's will. Name one plan you are making for this year. Ask others to pray for it, as Paul did. Then pray, ‘by God's will’, and mean it.
